prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Gradually, Into, What

outputs.L1:
Gradually, a girl’s innocence itself becomes her major crime.

A doe and her two fawns bent low in the sumac along the bank of a highway, the pinched peach of their ears twitching in the heat.

Into the disordered evening, my brother cut out only his face from every photograph in the hall, carefully slipping each frame back into position.

What good does it do? Decades of no faces other than our own chipping faces. What good does it do, this resemblance to nothing we know of the dollhouse?

New parents watch their newborn resting in a sunny patch of an empty room, the newborn making sense of its container—

And from the road, a deer ripened in death, and a tuft of fur—or dandelion—tumbled along, gently circled, driftwood, shaking loose, gathered, dissolving into the mouths of jewelweed nearby.

Earth is rife with iron, and blood is rich in stardust.

Immediately, I spotted one hoofprint, then nothing, as if this was where she dragged herself out of the body.

Strips of tire torn from their orbit.

Is it right, then, that we are left to hurtle alone?
outputs.L2: Little by little, a girl’s purity is treated as her gravest offense. Beside the highway, a doe and her pair of fawns crouched among the sumac, their ears—small, tightened peaches—flickering in the warmth. During the unsettled dusk, my brother removed only his own face from every picture in the hallway, then cautiously returned each frame to its place. What purpose did that serve? Years upon years without any faces except ours, our own features slowly flaking away. And what use is this likeness to nothing we recognize from the miniature house? First-time parents observe their infant lying in a bright square of sunlight in an otherwise vacant room, the child beginning to understand the space holding it. Out by the roadway, a deer had matured into death, while a clump of hair—or perhaps a dandelion—rolled past, softly wheeling like loose driftwood, trembling free, collecting and then vanishing into the mouths of the jewelweed close by. The ground abounds in iron; our blood carries an abundance of star matter. At once I found a single hoof mark, but no others followed, as though she had pulled herself from her own body at that exact spot. Shredded lengths of tire lay torn from their circular course. Is it fitting, then, that we should be abandoned to rush onward by ourselves?
outputs.L3:
The text portrays a girl’s gradual loss of innocence not as a natural part of growing up, but as something for which she is blamed—as though maturity itself were a kind of “crime.” This sense of guilt and estrangement is deepened by the brother’s attempt to erase himself from the family’s collective memory. By cutting his face out of every photograph, he does more than destroy images of himself: he creates visible absences in the family record, turning each photograph into evidence of both his former presence and his deliberate disappearance.

Throughout the text, physical imagery emphasizes the vulnerability of embodied life. Images of newborn existence are placed alongside the death of a deer, linking beginnings and endings through the fragility of the bodies that contain and define living beings. Human and animal life are further connected through recurring references to iron, blood, and stardust. Iron is at once a substance of the Earth and an element carried in blood, while stardust suggests that all bodies originate in the same cosmic matter. These images dissolve the boundaries between human beings, animals, the planet, and the wider universe, presenting life as a temporary arrangement of shared material.

Yet this sense of physical and cosmic connection does not necessarily provide emotional comfort. The text closes with uncertainty, asking whether such connections can truly relieve suffering or whether each individual must ultimately move through life alone. Its final question therefore leaves a tension unresolved: all beings may be materially bound to one another, but the experiences of pain, loss, and alienation may remain profoundly solitary.
outputs.L4:
The poem explores innocence, identity, family erasure, birth, and mortality through a series of fragmented, unsettling images. Photographs suggest an effort to preserve identity and family history, yet they also reveal absence: people can be cropped out, forgotten, or reduced to silent likenesses. In this context, innocence is precarious. The image of a newborn evokes beginnings, dependence, and the hope that a life might be protected, while also emphasizing how vulnerable every person is from the moment of birth.

Images of deer and roadside wreckage bring that vulnerability into a violent physical landscape. The deer represents natural grace and defenselessness, but its proximity to roads and collisions turns it into a figure of threatened life. Roadside remains suggest that movement itself carries danger and that bodies—human and animal alike—can be abruptly transformed into debris. The poem’s fractured form reinforces this sense of instability, linking birth and death, tenderness and brutality, without offering a secure narrative that could make those oppositions easier to understand.

Throughout the poem, physical resemblance and shared biological matter seem to promise connection. Family members may recognize themselves in one another, and all living beings participate in the same cycles of flesh, birth, injury, and decay. Yet these similarities cannot guarantee belonging or safety. A person can still be erased from a family image, abandoned within a history, or exposed to impersonal violence. Kinship exists, but it does not necessarily overcome isolation.

The poem therefore presents life as both deeply interconnected and irreducibly solitary. We are made from shared matter and surrounded by echoes of other lives, yet each body remains vulnerable to loss, accident, and death. The final idea of being left to “hurtle alone” gathers these tensions into a haunting conclusion: existence is motion without certainty, and neither resemblance, family, nor innocence can fully protect us from the forces that threaten to separate and destroy us.
outputs.L5: Gradually, we grow into what we are meant to become. Change rarely happens all at once; it begins quietly, through small choices, unexpected lessons, and moments of courage. We may not always know what lies ahead, but every step carries us into a new understanding of ourselves. In time, what once felt uncertain becomes part of who we are.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal, fragmented prose poem about family photographs, girlhood, deer by a highway, birth, death, and the loneliness of resemblance, using vivid natural imagery and minimal punctuation.
counterfactuals.output:
in the family photograph every woman has my mouth  
a small red door in winter  

mother at sixteen beneath the pear tree  
her white dress full of weather  
her hands not yet acquainted with blood  

behind her the dead stand politely  
blurred by rain  
each face a moon seen through milk  

I was born years later  
or earlier  
depending on which photograph is dreaming  

the hospital window opened onto a field of thistles  
my first cry lifted a flock of blackbirds  
my father held me like a letter  
addressed to someone missing  

girlhood was a house with green water in the mirrors  
braids damp as river roots  
knees jeweled with gravel  
the long afternoons molting their gold  

we drove north past the highway deer  
their bodies gathered at the edge of speed  
brown saints in the weeds  
flies bright as scattered beads  

one living doe watched from the median  
her eyes two dark rooms  
where every daughter waits  
for the mother to recognize her  

after the funeral we opened the albums  

grandmother in foxglove  
aunt in snow  
the baby who lived three hours  
wrapped in a blanket of tiny blue stars  

their faces leaned toward mine  
as trees lean over a drowned thing  

how lonely to resemble the dead  
to carry their unfinished weather  
the same cheekbone  
the same tilted grief  
the same pale animal startled behind the eyes  

at dusk the photographs loosen from their corners  
and wander into the grass  

girls become mothers  
mothers become ash  
the ash enters the river  
the river enters the deer  

and somewhere beside the highway  
under a sky bruised violet  
a newborn opens her mouth  

all our voices come out
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental elegy in one continuous paragraph that braids together a brother cutting his face from photographs, new parents watching their baby, and an injured doe disappearing near the road.
counterfactuals.output: My brother begins with the school pictures, the blunt scissors worrying a silver path around his cheek, and then the birthdays, the lake, our father’s funeral—each little face lifted out, leaving the family gathered around a white wound; across town, new parents lean over their sleeping baby as if attending the first small fire on earth, counting the blue commas of breath, touching one finger to the soft gate of the skull; dusk lowers itself beside the highway where an injured doe drags one dark leg through the sumac, pauses in the red wash of taillights, then enters the trees as though the trees had opened to receive her. We say gone when we mean beyond the frame. We say safe when the chest rises again. My brother mails me an album full of weather, shoulders embracing vacancy, candles illuminating no one, and in the margins his careful hand: I was here, I was here, I—; meanwhile the baby dreams milk into its fists, the parents keep vigil over that impossible future, and somewhere past the guardrail the doe lies down or keeps moving, blood threading the leaves with a map no photograph can hold. By morning, the road is empty; by morning, the cut faces have curled like pale petals in the trash; by morning, two exhausted bodies wake to a cry and call it life, call it grief’s bright animal returning, though nothing returns unchanged, though every love is a doorway the beloved is already passing through.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a lyrical collage poem exploring innocence as guilt, inherited identity, bodily mortality, and cosmic isolation; include jewelweed, sumac, tire strips, hoofprints, iron, blood, and stardust.
counterfactuals.output:
### **Inheritance, with Roadside Flowers**

I was born innocent—  
which is to say, already carrying  
the locked room, the missing key,  
my mother’s mouth inside my mouth  
saying *we did nothing*  
until nothing became a crime.

Along the ditch, jewelweed  
held its orange lanterns low.  
Sumac reddened like a family story  
no one survived telling cleanly.

We walked where tire strips  
lay shed from the highway—  
black skins, torn alphabets—  
and in the mud, hoofprints  
filled slowly with rain.

Whose animal passed here?  
Whose hunger wore my name?

In the body, iron keeps account.  
A nail’s dark grammar,  
a planet’s buried core—  
the same iron turning in blood  
as if the dead had left  
their small red coins behind.

I inherited the face  
but not the alibi.  
The hands, but not what they held.  
Even my bones testify  
in the language of minerals.

At night I press one palm  
against the other  
to feel how little warmth  
stands between being alive  
and having been alive.

Above me, stardust—  
our oldest inheritance—  
drifts through distances  
no prayer can cross.

The stars do not forgive us.  
They do not accuse.

They burn alone,  
and call it light.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a haunting contemporary poem in the style of associative eco-poetry, moving cinematically between domestic scenes and roadkill imagery and ending with a question about whether humans are destined to hurtle alone.
counterfactuals.output:
At 2 a.m. the refrigerator clicks awake,  
a small white animal worrying the dark.  
Milk clouds the glass. An onion  
keeps its many rooms closed.

Outside, rain edits the street  
into one long black sentence.  
A delivery van passes, blue-lit,  
carrying our hunger from door to door.

Morning: someone has folded  
the dish towel over the oven handle  
as if bandaging a wrist.  
In the sink, three spoons hold  
three distorted windows.

Then the highway opens—  
guardrails flashing like wet ribs,  
pines dragged backward by speed.  
On the shoulder, a fox  
has become an interruption:

red grammar, bright tail,  
one paw lifted  
as though the air were a door  
it had almost managed to knock on.

We do not stop.

The radio says oceans are warming.  
The radio says traffic ahead.  
A child in the back seat  
breathes a circle onto the glass  
and draws a house inside it:

roof, chimney, square of sun.  
Behind us, the fox diminishes  
to a rust-colored comma,  
then nothing the mirror can admit.

At home, we rinse lettuce,  
shake loose a little weather,  
watch an ant carry  
a white crumb across the counter  
with the patience of a planet.

Night arrives in plastic bags.  
We unpack peaches, soap,  
a chicken sealed beneath clear film.  
Somewhere, tires keep translating  
fur and feather into silence.

The refrigerator clicks awake again.  
The house floats on its wires.  
Beyond the curtains, lanes shine  
toward every vanishing point—

and are we destined  
to hurtle alone?
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a punctuation-light prose poem about faces erased from family history, a newborn learning the limits of a room, and deer along a highway, with recurring questions and dreamlike transitions.
counterfactuals.output:
who was she before the scissors  
before the album gave her face to the dark  

no one remembers  
or everyone remembers differently  

in the next room a newborn lifts one hand  
touches the pale border of morning  
finds the wall with an open palm  

is this where the world ends  
is this where the world begins  

the ceiling drifts above the crib  
a white field without weather  
then becomes a road at midnight  
then becomes the breath of deer  

they stand along the highway  
small moons opening in their eyes  
grass hanging from their mouths  
as if they have just spoken our names  

who called us here  
who failed to call us home  

behind them the trees wear the faces  
cut from every photograph  
an aunt without a year  
a brother folded into silence  
a child whose likeness survives  
only in the cheek of another child  

the newborn turns toward the window  
learning distance by losing it  
learning the room through hunger  
through shadow  
through the door that will not open  

is this where the world ends  
is this where the world begins  

we drive on  
or dream we drive on  
while the deer remain between departure and arrival  
their bodies lit briefly  
then erased by the dark  

and who will remember the dark  
who will give it a face
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
